## Introduction & background

Power architectures in modern hardware are complex trees of mixed topologies. Recognizing a buck, boost, or buck-boost converter simply by the placement of its inductor, switch, and diode is a baseline hardware engineering skill. Furthermore, system design requires architecting power trees that balance efficiency, noise, and cost. High-current digital rails demand switching converters, while sensitive analog sensors (like ADCs and RF front-ends) require the low ripple of an LDO.

## Activity

Paper. (1) Three schematics using the same three parts (switch, diode, inductor) rearranged — identify buck / boost / buck-boost purely from where the inductor sits, then verify each in Falstad. (2) Monty's design question, done for real: "2S LiPo in; rails: 5 V @ 1 A, 3.3 V @ 300 mA digital, 3.3 V @ 50 mA clean analog — design the power architecture," with topology per rail, estimated dissipation, and why the analog rail is an LDO hung off the 5 V buck. (3) Spot-the-bug: high-side N-FET with its gate driven 0/5 V while its source sits at the motor terminal — why does it never fully turn on?
